chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Profit and Loss Statement

lessons.title: Gross Margin, EBITDA and Operating Margin: Which Profit Number Matters for Your Team

children.text: In one meeting at Kesari Foods, three people quote three different margins. The sales head says the business runs at 48%. The CFO says 16%. The board deck says 7%. Nobody is lying, and all three numbers come from the same P&L.

They are quoting different rungs of the same ladder. Each rung strips out one more layer of cost, and each one is the right answer to a different question. Knowing which rung you are standing on is what separates a manager who argues from one who decides.

body.text: There is no such thing as "the margin". There is a ladder of margins, and your job is to know which rung your decision actually moves.

children.text: The Ladder, One Rung at a Time
Start at revenue and subtract costs in layers. Every rung has a name, a formula and an owner.

body.caption: The margin ladder
headers: What you subtract to get here

cells: The direct cost of making or buying what you sold
Do we make money on each unit we sell?
All remaining operating costs except depreciation and amortisation
Is the business itself generating a surplus?
Does it still work after we account for wear and tear on assets?
Anyone who signs off capital spending
Interest costs, after adding other income
Does it work given how we are funded?
What is left for the shareholders?

body.caption: Direct costs only: materials, and in some presentations direct labour and factory costs

body.latex: \text{EBITDA} = \text{Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation}
body.caption: Operating profit before the two biggest non-operating and non-cash charges
Every rung becomes a margin when divided by revenue

children.text: Climbing Down the Ladder at Kesari Foods
Take the FY25 statement from the previous lesson and work down it, rung by rung. Revenue is ₹50 crore.

body.caption: Kesari Foods FY25: from revenue to profit after tax (₹ crore)

cells: Less: materials consumed, net of inventory change
Add: other income, less finance costs

body.title: Where each ₹100 of Kesari Foods sales goes

children.text: That last slice is the point of the whole lesson. Out of every ₹100 of snacks sold, ₹52 goes straight back out to buy flour, oil and packaging, and ₹6.40 of sales income survives to the bottom. A one rupee change in material cost per ₹100 of sales moves the bottom line by roughly 16%.

body.title: Compute the EBITDA margin
body.prompt: A distributor reports revenue of ₹80 crore, cost of goods sold of ₹56 crore, employee costs of ₹9 crore and other operating expenses of ₹7 crore. Depreciation is ₹3 crore and interest is ₹2 crore. What is the EBITDA margin, in percent?
body.explanation: Gross profit = ₹80 crore minus ₹56 crore = ₹24 crore. EBITDA = ₹24 crore minus ₹9 crore minus ₹7 crore = ₹8 crore. Depreciation and interest sit below EBITDA, so they are ignored here. ₹8 crore ÷ ₹80 crore = 10%.

children.text: Which Rung Your Decision Actually Moves
Most workplace arguments about margin are really arguments about which rung the speakers are standing on.

body.caption: Your decision and the rung it moves

cells: Give a 5% discount to close a deal
Revenue falls while the cost of the goods does not
Switch to a cheaper packaging vendor
Direct material cost per unit falls
Hire four people in customer support
Operating cost rises with no change in cost per unit sold
Other expenses rise now, revenue may follow later
Depreciation rises for years, below EBITDA
Refinance the term loan at a lower rate
Only finance costs change, operations are untouched

body.text: This is why a discount hurts more than it looks. At a 48% gross margin, a 5% price cut does not cost you 5% of profit. It costs you about a tenth of the gross profit on every unit, because the cost side does not move at all.

body.title: Pricing a new customer
body.question: A distributor asks for a 4% price cut on a product that carries a 20% gross margin. Ignoring volume changes, what happens to the gross profit earned on each unit?
options: It is unchanged, because costs did not change
body.explanation: On ₹100 of price, gross profit is ₹20. Cutting price to ₹96 leaves gross profit of ₹16, since the ₹80 cost is unchanged. That is a fall of ₹4 on ₹20, which is 20% of the gross profit. The thinner your gross margin, the more damage a small discount does.

children.text: EBITDA: Useful, Popular and Easy to Abuse

EBITDA is the number you will hear most often in Indian boardrooms, investor calls and startup pitches. It is a rough proxy for the cash the operations throw off before funding decisions and accounting charges. It lets you compare two companies without their debt and asset ages getting in the way.

body.label: EBITDA is not an accounting standard
body.value: You will not find it in any Ind AS
body.context: No standard defines EBITDA, which is why companies present their own versions, including "adjusted EBITDA" that also excludes share-based payments, one-off costs or even routine items. Always check the definition footnote before you compare two companies.

body.title: The case for and against EBITDA

columns.label: Why people use it
points: Strips out interest, so funding choices do not distort the comparison
Strips out depreciation, which depends on when assets were bought
Closer to operating cash generation than net profit
Widely used, so benchmarks are easy to find

columns.label: Why it misleads
points: Ignores the cost of the assets a business must keep replacing
Ignores interest, which a leveraged company genuinely must pay
Ignores working capital, so it is not cash
Company-defined adjustments can quietly remove real costs

body.title: Why Ind AS 116 made EBITDA look better without anything improving

children.text: Before April 2019, rent on an office or store was a single operating expense sitting inside EBITDA. Under Ind AS 116, most leases became a right-of-use asset and a lease liability, so the rent line was replaced by depreciation on the asset and interest on the liability, both of which sit below EBITDA.
For a retail chain or an airline, this shifted a very large cost out of EBITDA overnight. Reported EBITDA rose sharply even though the business paid exactly the same rent as before.
When comparing across companies:
check they are on the same standard and the same lease treatment before you compare EBITDA margins.
When comparing across years:
a jump in EBITDA margin around FY20 in a lease-heavy business is usually accounting, not performance.
The practical fix:
for lease-heavy businesses, compare operating margin after depreciation, or look at cash from operations instead.

Margins also differ enormously by industry, so a number only means something against the right benchmark. For FY25, Britannia Industries earned an operating profit of ₹3,176 crore on revenue of ₹17,943 crore, an operating margin of 17.7%. Infosys earned ₹39,236 crore on ₹1,62,990 crore, a margin of 24.1%. A biscuit maker that hits 24% would be extraordinary. A software firm that falls to 17.7% would face hard questions.

body.title: What EBITDA leaves out
body.textWithBlank: EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, ___ and amortisation.
body.explanation: Depreciation is the annual charge for assets bought in earlier years. Excluding it makes an asset-heavy business look healthier than it is, which is exactly why capital-intensive companies like quoting EBITDA.

body.title: The festive discount plan
body.scenario: You are the marketing head at Kesari Foods. Gross margin is 48% and EBITDA margin is 16%. You propose a Diwali campaign: a 10% price cut on the flagship pack for two months, supported by ₹1.5 crore of extra advertising. Sales of that pack normally run at ₹12 crore over those two months. You expect volumes to rise 25%.
body.prompt: Work out what happens to gross profit and EBITDA, and decide whether to recommend it.
body.modelAnswer:
Base case for the two months: revenue ₹12 crore, gross profit at 48% is ₹5.76 crore.
With the plan:
1. Volumes rise 25%, so units sold go from 100 to 125. At a 10% lower price, revenue is ₹12 crore × 1.25 × 0.90 = ₹13.5 crore.
2. Material cost is 52% of the original price and does not change per unit, so cost rises with volume: ₹6.24 crore × 1.25 = ₹7.8 crore.
3. Gross profit becomes ₹13.5 crore minus ₹7.8 crore = ₹5.7 crore, marginally below the ₹5.76 crore base. Gross margin falls from 48% to about 42%.
4. Then subtract the ₹1.5 crore of extra advertising, which sits below gross profit. EBITDA is about ₹1.5 crore worse than the base case.
The recommendation: on these numbers the plan destroys profit even though revenue looks 12.5% higher. It needs either a smaller discount, a larger volume response, or a strategic reason such as blocking a competitor launch or winning shelf space that lasts beyond the two months. Present it with the volume response required to break even, so leadership can judge the risk rather than the story.

body.title: Find your own margins
steps: Take last year's P&L for your company and compute all four margins: gross, EBITDA, operating and net.
Write down which single rung your team's decisions move most often.
Find the same four margins for one listed competitor on screener.in.
Note any gap wider than two percentage points and identify the cost line behind it.
If your company leases a lot of space, check whether EBITDA comparisons are being distorted by lease accounting.
Ask your finance business partner which margin leadership is actually targeting this year.

points: Margins form a ladder: gross profit, EBITDA, operating profit, profit before tax and profit after tax. Each strips out one more layer of cost.
Gross margin answers whether each unit sold makes money. EBITDA answers whether the business generates a surplus. Operating margin adds the cost of using assets.
Match the rung to the decision: discounts and sourcing move gross margin, headcount and marketing move EBITDA, capital spending moves operating margin.
A small discount eats a large share of gross profit, because costs do not fall with price.
EBITDA is not defined by any accounting standard, so check how a company defines it before comparing.
Ind AS 116 moved lease costs below EBITDA, which flattered lease-heavy businesses without changing what they actually pay.

body.text: Kesari Foods is fictional. Britannia and Infosys figures are FY25 consolidated numbers as shown on screener.in, used only for industry comparison. Nothing here is investment advice.
